title: One Sugary Drink a Day More Than Doubles Stomach Cancer Risk, Landmark U.S. Study Finds
excerpt: Mass General Brigham researchers analyzed data from 112,000 adults over decades and found a 2.45 times higher risk of gastric cancer among daily consumers of sugar-sweetened beverages
body:
• People who drank at least one sugar-sweetened beverage daily had a 2.45 times higher risk of developing stomach cancer compared to those who rarely consumed them
  • The study — the first of its kind in a U.S. population — tracked 112,284 adults over decades and found 278 cases of gastric cancer
  • Artificially sweetened beverages were not associated with increased stomach cancer risk, and researchers say the findings point to sugar-specific biological mechanisms

Drinking just one sugar-sweetened beverage a day — a can of soda, a glass of lemonade, or a sports drink — may more than double your risk of developing stomach cancer, according to research published this month in the journal Gastro Hep Advances.

The study, led by researchers at the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, is the first to demonstrate an association between sugar-sweetened beverage consumption and gastric cancer in a U.S. population. With approximately 65% of American adults reporting they drink at least one such beverage daily, the findings carry broad public health implications.

The Study

Researchers analyzed data from 112,284 participants enrolled in two long-running research projects: the Nurses' Health Study, which began in 1976, and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, which started in 1986. Both collected detailed information on diet, lifestyle, and health outcomes over many years.

During the follow-up period, which spanned decades and covered more than 3.2 million person-years of observation, 278 participants developed gastric cancer.

The analysis found that people who consumed at least one sugar-sweetened beverage per day — including carbonated drinks, punch, lemonade, and sports drinks — had a 2.45 times higher risk of developing stomach cancer compared to those who drank less than one serving per month. Higher intake of fructose, the primary sweetener in these beverages, was also independently associated with increased gastric cancer risk.

"This is the first study to demonstrate an association between sugar-sweetened beverage intake and gastric cancer in a U.S. population. Gastric cancer is the fifth-leading cause of cancer death worldwide, but we've known very little about how diet might contribute to this cancer."

— Dr. Andrew Chan, Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute

Why Sugar, Not Artificial Sweeteners?

Notably, artificially sweetened beverages — such as diet sodas — were not associated with any increased risk of stomach cancer. Researchers believe the distinction points to sugar-specific biological pathways.

"It's possible that some of the mechanisms linking sugar-sweetened beverages to cancer, like the metabolic effects of fructose or the calorie load contributing to weight gain, simply don't apply to artificially sweetened beverages, since they don't contain the same sugars or calories," said Dr. Andrew Chan, the study's senior author and a gastroenterologist and epidemiologist at Mass General Brigham.

The researchers theorize that the elevated risk may be driven by weight gain, increased insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and changes to the gut microbiome — all of which have been linked to cancer development in previous studies. However, because the study was observational, it cannot establish a direct causal relationship.

The Broader Cancer Connection

Previous research has linked sugar-sweetened beverages to increased risks of colorectal, breast, and liver cancers. The new study extends that pattern to gastric cancer, which is the fifth most common cancer worldwide and often diagnosed at advanced stages when treatment options are limited.

"Unlike some cancers with established screening programs, there isn't a standard screening test for stomach cancer in the U.S.," Chan said. "Prevention through modifying risk factors such as diet is critical."

Anton Bilchik, a surgical oncologist at Providence Saint John's Cancer Institute in Santa Monica, California, who was not involved in the study, called the findings "alarming."

"The factor that seems to be one of the most important causes of cancer, whether it be stomach cancer or other forms of cancer, is inflammation," Bilchik said. "Whether sweetened drinks cause or result in increased inflammation and then stomach cancer is yet to be studied."

What Experts Recommend

For those looking to cut back, dietitian Meridan Zerner advises starting with one swap per day. "Replace one sugar-sweetened beverage with cold water, sparkling water, or unsweetened iced tea," she said. "Give yourself permission to taper rather than quit abruptly."

Zerner noted that sugary drinks extend well beyond soda — lemonade, smoothie drinks, and certain sports drinks also qualify. "Read the label. Check serving size and added sugars," she said.
